title: Limitations and reproducibility
section: Limitations and deviations from protocol v2
text:
Limitations and deviations from protocol v2

The seven-trial primary set includes one contrast-based trial and one subgroup-derived trial (APROCCHSS CAP subgroup, shock-only, 96% ventilated). The agent hierarchy has two populated clusters and agent is confounded with trial.
Heterogeneity (τ) and the agent SD (ω) are weakly identified; results depend on their half-Normal priors, as the sensitivity grid shows.
Model fitting uses cmdstanr (hybrid likelihood) because brms cannot combine a binomial and a contrast likelihood under one shared effect; brms reproduces the Stan results for the pure-count and pure-contrast cases (cross-check above). The protocol text names brms, so this is a documented deviation.
Sensitivity fits S-vi, S-viii and S-ix were added after protocol v2 (decisions logged 16 to 27 October 2026); S-ix and the SONIA agent-mix rule still need to be written into the registered text.
The one-dimensional tipping analysis reports where P(OR<1) falls below 0.90 and 0.80; an earlier draft of the protocol used different criteria.
RoB 2 is pending and GRADE is not done. The Pitre 2025 values are transcribed from the main text and supplement (some read from figure images) and need human verification against the original files.

How to read the comparison:

Effect scale. Pitre reports a risk ratio. The second row converts it to an odds ratio at their stated control risk of 17.5% with \(OR = RR(1-p)/(1-RR\,p)\); this is our approximation, not a value reported by the paper.
Time horizon and set. Pitre’s short-term mortality is described inconsistently in the paper (28 to 30 days in the abstract, “up to 60 days” in the methods, “30 to 60 days” in Table 2) and covers 29 trials; our F4 (17 trials) is the nearest set in scope, and F1 is the severe-only set. Patient numbers for our fits count only trials with arm-level counts, so the REMAP-CAP contrast trial adds none.
No severe-only comparator. Neither the main text nor the supplement gives a severe-only mortality estimate (the supplement stratifies by primary trial population: ARDS, pneumonia, sepsis), so F1 cannot be compared like for like.
Estimates. Our F4 OR is 0.74 (0.55–0.95), against 0.79 (0.70–0.89) for the converted Pitre estimate. The F4 interval is wider, as expected with 17 rather than 29 trials.
Absolute scale. Pitre report 31 fewer deaths per 1000 at a control risk of 17.5%; our F4 gives 39 per 1000 at 17.4%, and our severe-CAP set F1 gives 54 per 1000 at a higher control risk of 19.8%, with an interval that includes no effect.

title: Benchmark against Pitre 2025
section: Why the probabilities differ: the Bayesian models are not the same
text:
Why the probabilities differ: the Bayesian models are not the same
The supplement (Table S2) shows that Pitre’s Bayesian analysis is a common-effect (fixed-effect) normal model on the log scale: each trial’s estimate is normal around a single true effect θ with a vague Normal(0, precision 0.0001) prior and no between-trial variance term, fitted in rjags. Trials with infinite log effects, that is trials with a zero event count, are dropped. Table S2 also defines the “OR” as the ratio of event proportions (which is a risk ratio) while using the standard error of a log odds ratio. Our model is random-effects with exact binomial likelihoods, so zero-event trials stay in and between-trial heterogeneity widens the posterior.
This matters for the headline numbers. Pitre’s P(OR<1) is 0.995 and P(OR<0.9) is 0.868. Applying their method to our F4 count trials (14 of 16 count trials remain after dropping zero-event trials) gives 0.82 (0.71–0.94) with P(OR<1) = 0.998 and P(OR<0.9) = 0.913, close to their own result, whereas our random-effects F4 fit gives P(OR<1) = 0.988 and P(OR<0.9) = 0.942. For the severe-CAP set F1 the same pair is 0.993 (common-effect, five count trials, REMAP-CAP and Confalonieri excluded) against 0.949 (our primary model). Fitting a common-effect model to our own data with the exact binomial likelihood (REMAP-CAP as a contrast, zero-event trials kept; the S-CE sensitivity fits) gives P(OR<1) of 0.999 for F1 and 1.000 for F4, so removing between-trial heterogeneity alone brings our probabilities to the level of Pitre’s. Much of the gap between the probabilities is therefore a model choice, mainly the assumption of no heterogeneity, not a difference in the data. Pitre’s frequentist random-effects analysis also finds little heterogeneity (overall I² 4.1%, τ² 0 on the risk-ratio scale; Figures S18 to S24), whereas our heterogeneity is poorly identified (F1 median τ 0.47, F4 0.28, with intervals that include values near zero). Dropping Confalonieri, the trial with the strongest raw effect, is a further difference between the two approaches.
The supplement’s long-term result (P(OR<0.9) = 0.7802, Table S25) differs slightly from the 78.7% in the main text; we use the supplement table.

Both analyses give hydrocortisone the lower point estimate (Pitre 0.66 as a risk ratio, ours 0.66 as an odds ratio) and methylprednisolone a higher one, and both find that the agent differences are not statistically distinguishable (their test for subgroup differences p = 0.27; our P(hydrocortisone more favourable) = 0.68). Other supplement analyses relevant to ours:

By primary population (Figures S21 and S22). Their pneumonia stratum (19 estimates, REMAP-CAP coded as ARDS) gives RR 0.75 (0.59–0.95) (τ² 0.04, I² 17%), and 0.79 (0.62–1.01) (τ² 0.07, I² 26%) when REMAP-CAP is coded as pneumonia. Coding REMAP-CAP in the pneumonia stratum moves the upper bound of the interval from just below 1 to just above 1, which mirrors the sensitivity of our F1 result to REMAP-CAP (see the sensitivity page). The pneumonia stratum is the closest in content to our F3 and F4.
By risk of bias (Figure S24). Low-risk trials (20) give RR 0.80 (0.71–0.91) and high-risk trials (11) give 0.71 (0.46–1.10) (difference p = 0.59). Our own low-risk-of-bias analysis (S-ii) cannot be run until RoB 2 judgements exist.
Dose-response (Table S20). Their non-linear model gives risk ratios of 0.84, 0.78, 0.71 at 40, 60 and 80 mg/day prednisone-equivalent, with wide intervals at the highest doses (RR at 100 mg/day 0.66 (0.41–1.05)). Our meta-regressions point the same way (higher dose, more benefit; F4 -0.23 (-0.80 to 0.32) per SD of dose) but with intervals that include no effect, and our F1 dose coefficient rests on five trials spanning 50 to 60 mg/day.

These are candidates for the row-by-row extraction check.
The trial sets, scales, weights and priors all differ, so the comparison is a face-validity check, not a replication.

title: Model checking
text:
Cross-check against brms
To confirm that the Stan hybrid model reproduces standard software when one likelihood is switched off, each case was refitted in brms (cmdstanr backend, same priors, 4 chains with 2000 post-warmup draws, adapt_delta 0.99):

Pure-count: F1 and F4 with the REMAP-CAP contrast removed, events | trials(n) ~ 0 + trial + trt + (0 + trt | trial) (unpooled trial baselines; trt is the pooled log-OR and the random-slope SD is τ).
Pure-contrast: the S-iii rows for F1 and F4 (every trial as log-OR and SE; Hagman, a double-zero trial, is dropped in F4), yi | se(sei) ~ 1 + (1 | trial).

Agreement was judged against a criterion fixed before looking at the results, in units of the pooled posterior SD of each quantity: means and medians within 0.10 SD and 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles within 0.20 SD (Monte Carlo error alone is of the order 0.02 to 0.05 SD, larger in the tails). It was assessed for μ, τ and every shrunken trial effect θ.


Code

title: Sensitivity analyses
text:
What moves the estimate

Handling of REMAP-CAP is the largest single influence on the median. Excluding it gives an OR of 0.60 (0.33–0.97) with P(OR<1) = 0.98, the lowest median OR of all F1 fits; using the ICU-discharge contrast instead of the day-90 contrast changes little (0.67 (0.39–1.05)), and the assumed SE of its contrast shifts P(OR<1) between 0.94 (SE 0.30) and 0.96 (SE 0.45).
Heterogeneity prior. A tighter τ prior narrows the interval (0.70 (0.48–1.01)), a wider one widens it (0.67 (0.32–1.23)), with the median essentially unchanged. The interval therefore depends on a prior that the seven trials cannot pin down.
Agent model. Letting the two agent clusters differ widely (ω prior SD 0.5) lowers P(OR<1) to 0.84 and widens the interval to 0.72 (0.35–1.55), the least favourable of the F1 fits, because uncertainty about agent effects feeds into the pooled estimate.
Dropping single trials by design. Removing APROCCHSS (subgroup-derived and the only mineralocorticoid trial; S-vi and S-viii are identical in F1) gives 0.70 (0.34–1.25), and removing the single-bolus Marik trial gives 0.70 (0.39–1.17). P(OR<1) is 0.90 and 0.93 respectively, against 0.95 for the default: a modest loss of certainty, with no change in direction.
Baseline prior and IPD rows. A tighter baseline prior (0.67 (0.38–1.09)) and replacing four trials’ counts with the Smit 2025 IPD rows (0.67 (0.39–1.04)) leave the result essentially unchanged.
Likelihood. The contrast-based fit S-iii, which replaces the exact binomial likelihood with a log-OR and SE, gives 0.74 (0.45–1.16), a higher median than the primary fit. It is the only fit that does not use the exact binomial likelihood, so the gap indicates how much the normal approximation and the continuity correction for Confalonieri’s zero cell matter with trials this small.
Common-effect model. Fixing τ near zero (no between-trial heterogeneity) while keeping the exact likelihood gives 0.70 (0.56–0.88) in F1 with P(OR<1) = 0.999. The median barely moves, but the interval narrows sharply and the probability of benefit rises to nearly 1, because the model treats the disagreement between trials as pure sampling noise. This is the assumption behind the much higher probabilities in Pitre’s Bayesian analysis (see the benchmark page); we regard the random-effects result as the appropriate primary analysis because the trials differ in design, dose, agent and population.
Larger sets. Dropping the subgroup-derived trials from F4 gives 0.75 (0.50–1.01) and using IPD rows in F4 gives 0.74 (0.54–0.93), both close to the F4 result (0.74 (0.55–0.95)); the common-effect F4 fit gives 0.77 (0.67–0.89).

Taken together, the direction of the estimate is stable (every F1 sensitivity fit has a median OR below 1), but the strength of the evidence varies: P(OR<1) falls to 0.84 in the least favourable fit.

title: Sensitivity analyses
text:
Notes on individual analyses

S-ii (low risk of bias only) has not been run: RoB 2 judgements are pending for all trials, so the code is a stub that stops until they are supplied.
S-iii converts each count trial to a log-OR and SE, adding 0.5 to all four cells of any trial with a zero cell (Confalonieri) and dropping double-zero trials. It is the only fit that uses a continuity correction; the forest plot on the results page also adds 0.5 to Confalonieri’s raw estimate, for display only.
S-CE is a common-effect sensitivity fit: the same model with the between-trial SD forced near zero through a very tight half-Normal(0, 0.001) prior, run in F1, F3 and F4.
S-iv varies the τ prior (half-Normal SD 0.25 and 1) and, in the agent model, the ω prior (SD 0.5).
S-v uses a tighter baseline prior, Normal(0, 2), instead of Normal(0, 10).
S-vi, S-viii and S-ix drop the subgroup-derived trial (APROCCHSS; in F4 also Tongyoo), the mineralocorticoid trial (APROCCHSS) and the single-bolus short-course trial (Marik).
S-IPD replaces rank-1 rows with Smit 2025 IPD rank-2 rows (cross-check only; never merged with the rank-1 row for the same trial).

This page reports the pooled effect of corticosteroids on short-term mortality as an odds ratio (OR); values below 1 favour corticosteroids. F1 is the primary analysis: seven severe-CAP trials, with REMAP-CAP entering as an adjusted contrast. F2 uses 90-day mortality, F3 adds the published severe subgroups of all-hospitalised trials, and F4 adds the whole-trial results of all hospitalised-CAP trials. All fits here use the reference prior N(0, 1) on the log-OR; other priors are on the priors page. Credible intervals (CrI) are 95% quantile intervals; “P(OR<x)” is the posterior probability that the pooled OR is below x.

title: Primary results
text:
Primary analysis (F1)
The pooled OR is 0.68 (0.38–1.10), with P(OR<1) = 0.95, P(OR<0.833) = 0.82 and P(OR>1.1) = 0.02. The between-trial SD has a posterior median of 0.47 (95% CrI 0.07–1.05), so it is poorly identified with seven trials. The predictive OR for a new trial is 0.68 (0.18–2.28).
The 95% credible interval includes 1, so the data are compatible with no effect, but most of the posterior probability lies below 1 (P(OR<1) = 0.95). The probability of an odds reduction of about 17% or more (OR<0.833) is 0.82, and the probability of a harmful effect of 10% or more in the odds (OR>1.1) is 0.02. The predictive interval is wider than the credible interval because it adds the between-trial variation: a new trial could plausibly show an effect on either side of 1, and the probability that its true OR is below 1 is 0.78.

In practical terms, hydrocortisone (five trials, including REMAP-CAP and APROCCHSS) has the lower point estimate (OR 0.66) and methylprednisolone (two trials, ESCAPe and Torres) a higher one (OR 0.75), but the two intervals overlap almost completely, and the probability that hydrocortisone is truly the more favourable agent is only 0.68. Because each trial used one agent, agent differences cannot be separated from trial differences in dose, timing and population. The result is a quantified shrinkage estimate, not evidence for or against an agent effect.

title: Bayesian meta-analysis of adjunctive corticosteroids in severe community-acquired pneumonia
text:
Abstract
Background. Randomised evidence on adjunctive systemic corticosteroids in severe community-acquired pneumonia (sCAP) is conflicting: hydrocortisone reduced 28-day mortality in CAPE COD, whereas ESCAPe (prolonged methylprednisolone) and REMAP-CAP (hydrocortisone, adaptive platform) did not show a benefit.
Methods. Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis of short-term all-cause mortality on the odds-ratio scale. Trials reporting arm counts enter through an exact binomial likelihood with unpooled trial baselines; REMAP-CAP, whose crude counts are not valid for pooling, enters as an adjusted contrast. The primary set (F1) has seven severe-CAP trials; broader sets cover 90-day mortality (F2), published severe subgroups (F3) and all hospitalised CAP (F4). We also fitted an agent-level hierarchy, a ladder of priors from enthusiastic to harm-leaning with tipping-point analyses, sensitivity fits and meta-regressions, and checked the model on simulated data and against brms. Four analysis decisions (D1 to D4) are unconfirmed, so pre-specified defaults are used and their alternatives are shown.
Results. In F1 the pooled odds ratio for death was 0.68 (0.38–1.10) (posterior median and 95% credible interval, reference prior). The posterior probability of any benefit (OR<1) was 0.95 and of an odds reduction of about 17% or more (OR<0.833) was 0.82. At the pooled control risk of 19.8% the absolute risk reduction was 5.4 percentage points (95% credible interval -1.5 to 11.2). Estimates were similar in the broader sets (F3: 0.74 (0.49–1.05); F4: 0.74 (0.55–0.95)). Between-trial heterogeneity was poorly identified (median τ 0.47), and the predictive odds ratio for a new trial was 0.68 (0.18–2.28). Across 13 sensitivity fits the pooled OR ranged from 0.60 to 0.74 and P(OR<1) from 0.84 to 1.00; excluding REMAP-CAP gave the lowest pooled OR, and a common-effect model without between-trial heterogeneity gave the highest probability of benefit (P(OR<1) 1.00). With a skeptical prior P(OR<1) was 0.92; with the two harm-leaning priors the posterior median OR was 0.89 and 0.86 and P(OR<1) was 0.76 and 0.75. The agent hierarchy could not separate hydrocortisone (OR 0.66) from methylprednisolone (OR 0.75; probability that hydrocortisone is more favourable 0.68), and the meta-regressions were uninformative.
Conclusions. Under the pre-specified defaults the data point towards lower short-term mortality with corticosteroids in sCAP, but not conclusively: the credible interval for the primary estimate includes no effect, the estimate depends on how REMAP-CAP is handled and on the prior, and four analysis decisions, risk-of-bias assessment and the REMAP-CAP standard error are still outstanding. These results are provisional.






TipPlain-language summary



The question. Do steroid medicines, such as hydrocortisone, given alongside antibiotics help adults with severe pneumonia caught outside hospital to survive?
What we did. We combined the results of the randomised trials that tested this in people with severe pneumonia. In these trials, patients were assigned by chance to receive a steroid or not, which makes the groups comparable. Seven trials form the main analysis.
What we found. In the comparison groups about 20 in 100 patients died. Our best estimate is that steroids lowered this by about 5 deaths per 100 patients treated, but this is uncertain: the plausible range runs from about 1.5 more deaths to about 11.2 fewer deaths per 100 patients treated. The analysis puts the chance that steroids lower the risk of dying at about 95 in 100.
Why it is not settled. The trials do not agree. Two of the larger ones (CAPE COD and APROCCHSS) found fewer deaths with hydrocortisone, while another (ESCAPe) and the large platform trial REMAP-CAP did not. The answer also depends on how REMAP-CAP is counted and on how skeptical one is to begin with: starting from a prior belief that steroids might do harm, the chance of benefit falls to about 75 in 100. We cannot tell which steroid works best.
What this means. This is a draft analysis, not a treatment recommendation. Several decisions, the checks on trial quality and one key number from REMAP-CAP are still to be settled, so these results may change.

title: Methods
text:
Model and sampling

Model. One-stage random-effects model on the log-OR with a hybrid likelihood: exact binomial for count trials and a normal likelihood for REMAP-CAP, which enters only as an adjusted contrast (log-OR 0.445, SE 0.362). Trial baselines are unpooled fixed effects with an N(0, 10) prior. Implemented in Stan (stan/hybrid_ma.stan) via cmdstanr; the protocol text names brms, so this is a documented deviation.
Fits. F1 primary short-term (7 trials), F2 90-day (3), F3 broad-severe (10), F4 all-hospitalised (17); F1 with an agent hierarchy; prior ladder; tipping-point analyses; sensitivity fits; meta-regressions.
Sampling. 4 chains × 2000 post-warmup draws, adapt_delta 0.99, max_treedepth 12, seed 7291. A fit is accepted only if R-hat < 1.01, bulk and tail ESS > 400 and there are zero divergences.
Priors. Pooled log-OR μ: Normal(0, 1) in the main fits (the reference rung), with the alternatives on the prior ladder page; between-trial SD τ ~ half-Normal(0, 0.5); between-agent SD ω ~ half-Normal(0, 0.25); trial baselines Normal(0, 10). The sensitivity page varies τ, ω and the baseline prior.
Quantities. Posterior median OR with a 95% quantile credible interval (CrI; HDI columns are in the downloadable tables), P(OR<1), P(OR<0.9), P(OR<0.833), P(OR>1.1), τ, the predictive OR for a new trial, and the absolute risk reduction (ARR) and number needed to treat (NNT). OR < 0.833 (= 1/1.2) is an odds ratio for survival of at least 1.2, that is a reduction of about 17% in the odds of death; it is the threshold REMAP-CAP used in its futility rule.

p_wide <- min(tip2$P_OR_lt_1[tip2$prior_sd >= 0.5])
above1 <- tip2[tip2$OR_median > 1, ]


In these maps each cell is one fit: the horizontal axis is the centre of the prior (as an OR; values above 1 mean the prior expects harm), the vertical axis its SD (small means confident). For priors centred on benefit or no effect (OR 0.70 to 0.90) P(OR<1) is at least 0.94 at every SD. A harm-leaning prior changes the conclusion only when it is also confident: with a centre of 1.25 or more and an SD of 0.2 or less, P(OR<1) is 0.57 or lower, whereas with an SD of 0.5 or more it stays at or above 0.83 for every centre. The posterior median OR exceeds 1 only for priors centred at 1.10 or higher with an SD of 0.20 or less. In other words, only a prior that is both centred on harm and held with considerable confidence stops the data from pointing toward benefit.

title: Discussion
text:
Principal findings
In the primary analysis of seven severe-CAP trials, corticosteroids were associated with lower short-term mortality: pooled OR 0.68 (0.38–1.10), with a posterior probability of any benefit of 0.95. The estimate is probable rather than established. The credible interval includes 1, the median absolute risk reduction of 5.4 percentage points has an interval from -1.5 to 11.2 points, and the predictive interval for a new trial (0.68 (0.18–2.28)) comfortably includes harm. The broader sets point the same way (F3 0.74 (0.49–1.05); F4 0.74 (0.55–0.95)), with the F4 interval excluding 1, but F4 answers a wider question and mixes severe and non-severe populations.
The uncertainty largely reflects disagreement between the trials. Raw odds ratios are below 1 for Marik 1993, Confalonieri 2005, Torres 2015, Dequin 2023 (CAPE COD), Heming 2024 (APROCCHSS) and at or above 1 for Meduri 2022 (ESCAPe), Heming 2025 (REMAP-CAP). This pattern matches the published narrative of a benefit in CAPE COD, no benefit in ESCAPe and a harm-leaning result in REMAP-CAP. A random-effects model cannot say why the trials differ, only how much they do; here the between-trial SD is moderate (median 0.47) but poorly identified, because there are only seven trials.

The role of REMAP-CAP
REMAP-CAP is, together with ESCAPe, the most influential trial in the analysis: leaving out either lowers the pooled median OR to about 0.60 (REMAP-CAP) or 0.60 (ESCAPe), and how REMAP-CAP is handled is a judgement call. Its crude counts cannot be pooled (response-adaptive randomisation, non-equipoise sites, control crossover), so its adjusted day-90 contrast enters F1 even though F1 is a short-term analysis, and its standard error is still an interim value derived from the published credible interval. Excluding REMAP-CAP gives 0.60 (0.33–0.97), with P(OR<1) = 0.98; varying the contrast’s SE from 0.30 to 0.45 moves P(OR<1) between 0.94 and 0.96. The investigator-supplied SE and the choice of REMAP-CAP timepoint (D2) will therefore matter for the final result. The question of what REMAP-CAP should contribute to a short-term estimate is a design question for the review, not something the data can settle.


Agent, dose and trial characteristics
The agent hierarchy was intended to ask whether hydrocortisone differs from other agents without the pitfalls of subgrouping. It cannot answer that here. Hydrocortisone has the lower point estimate (0.66 against 0.75 for methylprednisolone) but the probability that it is truly the more favourable agent is only 0.68, the between-agent SD stays at its prior, and each trial used a single agent, so agent is confounded with every other trial characteristic. The meta-regressions are no more informative: 22 were fitted, only 1 has an interval excluding zero (the F1 dose coefficient, which rests on five trials spanning 50 to 60 mg/day prednisone-equivalent and is not a dose-response estimate), and about that many would be expected by chance.


Sensitivity to the prior and to modelling choices
The conclusion is moderately robust to the prior. A skeptical prior reduces P(OR<1) only to 0.92, and on the tipping-point analysis P(OR<1) stays above 0.90 for skeptical priors with an SD of 0.30 or wider. Harm-leaning priors pull the posterior median to 0.89 and 0.86, still below 1, with a probability of benefit of about three in four; only a prior that is both centred on harm and held confidently reverses the direction. The 90-day set is more fragile: under the same harm-leaning priors its median OR is close to 1 (0.96 and 0.98), reflecting three trials and the weight of REMAP-CAP. Across the F1 sensitivity analyses the median OR never exceeds 0.74. Forcing the between-trial SD to zero (a common-effect model, as in Pitre’s Bayesian analysis) leaves the median almost unchanged (0.70 (0.56–0.88) in F1) but raises P(OR<1) to 0.999, which shows how much of the stated uncertainty comes from allowing the trials to differ.

title: Discussion
text:
Comparison with other syntheses
The closest published synthesis is Pitre et al. 2025 (29 trials with short-term mortality, RR 0.82 (0.74–0.91)). Converted to an odds ratio at their stated control risk, their estimate (0.79 (0.70–0.89)) is close to our F4 result and to the F3 and F1 intervals, which are wider and extend above 1. Pitre report a probability of 0.87 that the OR is below 0.9; ours is 0.89 for F1 and 0.94 for F4. The two analyses differ in trial set, effect scale, time horizon and priors, and Pitre do not report a severe-only mortality estimate in the main text or the supplement, so no like-for-like comparison for severe CAP is possible. A large part of the gap in probabilities is a modelling difference: the supplement shows their Bayesian analysis is a common-effect model with a vague prior that drops zero-event trials, and applying that method to our F4 count trials gives P(OR<1) of 0.998, much closer to their 0.995 than our random-effects 0.988. Their agent subgroups also give hydrocortisone the lower estimate without a clear difference between agents, in line with our agent hierarchy. Pitre also include Lloyd 2019, a stepped-wedge trial of a bundled intervention that our protocol excludes because the corticosteroid effect cannot be isolated. We have not yet compared our results with the Briel 2018 individual-patient-data analysis.

title: Discussion
text:
Strengths

The likelihood is exact for sparse count data (no continuity corrections in the primary fit) and a contrast likelihood is used for the one trial whose valid estimate is an adjusted contrast.
Trial baselines are unpooled, and a pooled-baseline comparison model gives a total held-out predictive log density of -22.2 against -22.7 for the primary model (difference 0.5, SE 0.3), so this choice does not appear to drive the results.
The model was validated on simulated data and reproduced by an independent implementation in brms (53 of 53 compared parameters within a pre-stated tolerance).
Prior influence is reported explicitly (ladder, one- and two-dimensional tipping points) rather than through a single analysis, and decisions that belong to the project lead are shown with their alternatives.
The whole analysis is reproducible from a single pipeline, so a corrected data row triggers only the affected fits.

title: Discussion
text:
Limitations

Few trials, heterogeneous contributions. The primary set has seven trials, one contrast-based and one subgroup-derived (APROCCHSS, a shock-only population, 96% ventilated). Its short-term outcome mixes ICU mortality (Marik), in-hospital mortality (Confalonieri, Torres, ESCAPe), day-28 mortality (CAPE COD, APROCCHSS) and, for REMAP-CAP, day-90 mortality. This is by rule, but the timepoints are not identical.
Open inputs. Risk of bias has not been assessed (19 of 19 trials pending, so the low-risk-of-bias sensitivity analysis could not be run), the REMAP-CAP SE is interim, screening was a single AI-assisted pass, extraction has had a numeric second check but not a row-by-row sign-off, and one pre-specified IPD replacement could not be done for two trials that have no IPD row in the dataset.
Aggregate data. The analysis uses published aggregate data, so effect modification by patient characteristics cannot be examined, and the meta-regressions are across-trial (ecological) analyses.
Possible missing trials. Some registered trials are unpublished or ongoing, and publication bias cannot be assessed formally with this few trials.
Heterogeneity and agent priors. Results depend on half-Normal priors for τ and ω that the data cannot fully inform; the sensitivity analysis shows the interval but not the median is affected.
Draft status. The report is AI-assisted, has not been peer reviewed, and the review is not yet registered.

title: Discussion
text:
Implications and next steps
These results do not by themselves support a clinical recommendation. They do suggest which pieces of information would matter most for a final analysis: the REMAP-CAP adjusted effect and its standard error, the day-28 or in-hospital definition for ESCAPe (D1), the prior ladder (D3), and the risk-of-bias judgements. A larger body of severe-CAP trials, particularly any that report a pre-specified 28-day or in-hospital mortality and a common set of timepoints, would reduce the dependence on τ and the prior. Because the pipeline is parameterised by the data file, each of these changes is a re-run rather than a rebuild.

title: Discussion
text:
Conclusion
Under the pre-specified defaults, the available randomised evidence leans towards lower short-term mortality with corticosteroids in severe community-acquired pneumonia (OR about 0.68, probability of any benefit 0.95). That conclusion is not secure: the primary interval includes no effect, it depends on how the adaptive REMAP-CAP trial is handled and on the prior, the agent question is unresolved, and several inputs are outstanding. The estimate should be treated as provisional.
